meta.title: The Empty Wall Beside the Picture
meta.theme: why the bare wall a gallery leaves around a painting is part of how the painting is seen

format.format_verified: 2026-09: four-sentence TITA jumble, the modern CAT default; re-verify against each new official paper

meta.learning_objective: resist joining two sentences because they share a word, and let 'In fact' and 'therefore' place the argument instead

quality.adversarial_review: The live rival joins the two sentences that both speak of the wall, putting the closing sentence about a curator's decisions straight after the opening complaint about wasted space. It breaks twice: that sentence contains 'therefore', which needs an argument in front of it and would have none, and the sentence beginning 'In fact' would then be correcting the curator rather than the visitor, when the mistaken impression it answers belongs to the visitor. The sentence about hanging two pictures close together cannot open, since its point is only visible once a claim about emptiness has been made for it to test.

source.usage_note: Original composition in CAT register for CAT OS. General writing on display and curation; no specific text adapted. Personal study only.

meta.reviewer_notes: A foundation-tier argumentative jumble whose only difficulty is a repeated noun. 'Wall' appears in the first and last sentences of the correct order, which invites a solver to glue them; the connectives override the repetition. Written to teach that a shared word is a hypothesis, not a link.

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: In fact the emptiness is doing work: it tells the eye where one painting ends and the next begins.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: A curator's hardest decisions are therefore about distance, and the wall that seems to hold nothing is holding one picture apart from another.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: Hang two pictures close together and they begin to argue: the reds of one pull at the reds of the other, and neither is seen on its own terms.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Visitors often take the bare stretches of wall in a gallery for wasted space, or for a sign that the collection is a thin one.

links.explanation: A opens with 'In fact', which corrects a mistaken impression. D supplies the impression in so many words: visitors take the bare wall for wasted space.
A claims that the emptiness separates one painting from the next. C is the test of that claim: take the emptiness away, hang two pictures close, and watch them interfere with each other.
B's 'therefore' draws the conclusion from the experiment in C, and its closing phrase, the wall that seems to hold nothing, returns to the bare stretches the paragraph began by defending.

explanation.macro_pattern_note: This is a small argument in four moves: a common mistake, the correction, the evidence for the correction, and the consequence for whoever hangs the pictures. The correction is marked by 'In fact' and the consequence by 'therefore', which is why the paragraph can be assembled without knowing anything about galleries.

movement.label: D
movement.why_here: D states the view the paragraph exists to answer. It needs nothing before it, and everything after it is addressed to the visitors it describes.

movement.label: A
movement.why_here: A is the turn. 'In fact' announces that a wrong impression is being corrected, and the impression is the one D has just reported.

movement.label: C
movement.why_here: C shows what happens when the emptiness A defends is removed. Evidence follows the claim it supports, and this evidence is unintelligible before the claim.

movement.label: B
movement.why_here: B draws the consequence for the curator and closes the loop back to the bare wall. Its 'therefore' means it cannot stand before the argument it concludes.

tempting_orders.why_tempting: Two sentences talk about the wall, one calling it wasted space and one calling it a wall that seems to hold nothing. The repetition looks like a join, and the second sentence answers the first so neatly that it feels designed to follow it.
tempting_orders.where_it_breaks: That sentence contains 'therefore'. Placed second, it concludes an argument that has not been made, and the sentence beginning 'In fact' would then be correcting a conclusion rather than the visitors' mistake. Repetition suggested the pair; the connective forbids it.

explanation.trap_named: The trap is the repeated noun. Setters place the same word in two sentences that must not touch, because a reader under time pressure joins on vocabulary before reading for function. A shared word tells you two sentences belong in the same paragraph; only a connective or a reference tells you they belong side by side.
explanation.solving_habit: When two sentences share a striking word, treat the pairing as a guess and then look for a connective that confirms or refuses it. 'Therefore' and 'In fact' are stronger evidence than any amount of repeated vocabulary.

mentor.challenge: Two sentences here speak of the same bare wall, and they must not be neighbours. One small word in each will tell you why.
mentor.paragraph_plain: People walking round a gallery often think the blank wall between pictures is a waste, or that the museum has not got enough to show. It is not a waste: the gap is what lets your eye tell one picture from the next. Put two paintings close together and they start to interfere, the colours of each pulling at the other, so that you cannot look at either by itself. That is why deciding how far apart to hang things is the hardest part of a curator's job, and why the wall that appears to hold nothing is in fact holding two pictures apart.
mentor.takeaway: Sentences that share a word are not necessarily neighbours; a connective outranks a repetition every time.
